vignette: Eileen, a 75-year-old Oceania-born woman who had spent much of her adult life working as an auditor, described how the war had entered her life in the ordinary, humiliating spaces where she had once tried to keep order. During a bombing in the city where she was living as a civilian, she became separated from her husband in the confusion and spent hours moving through damaged streets and crowded shelters, trying to account for people and papers while the smell of sweat, unwashed bodies, dust, and fear clung to the air. She said that when she thinks of it now, the memory comes back “like photographs,” fixed and stark, and yet she cannot find words for what happened in a way that feels adequate; she knows it happened, but the experience sits in her mind as vivid scenes and sensations rather than a story she can tell. The smell of sweat or body odour, even now in a busy room, can throw her back into those images, and moments of feeling happy or relaxed can do the same, because she becomes abruptly aware of how vulnerable she was when she had briefly let herself feel safe. When that smell catches her off guard, the feeling is not only that the war is back but that she should have known better than to relax at all, and it immediately feeds her conviction that she is permanently marked by what happened and that other people can see it on her. Those reminders have fed the thought that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her, as if the terror were written on her face, and she has come to believe that her life is not worth living anymore and that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again. Since then, Eileen has become preoccupied with what the event meant and how it might have been avoided. She goes over and over, in a painstaking and self-reproaching way, why it happened to her and how she might have prevented it, replaying every decision from the day of the attack, every route she took, every delay, and every choice she made while trying to preserve a sense of control. That rumination keeps the scene alive in a vividly visual form: the more she searches for a reason, the more she sees those same photographic fragments, and the more she tries to put the experience into words, the more the images take over. The act of thinking it through has only deepened her sense that something terrible was exposed in her, something others can detect immediately, and it has strengthened her belief that she is changed in a permanent, visible way. That conviction of being permanently altered kept pulling the memory back into focus, as if she had to look at it again and again to confirm the proof of her failure. Each return made the scenes feel more vivid and harder to shake, not less. At night she often lies awake reviewing it all, and the memory of the event is intensified rather than settled by this effort to explain it. She had also learned, without quite naming it, to keep herself busy and to avoid quiet moments so the images would not get a foothold; silence and stillness had become things to outmanoeuvre, not rest in. Her sense of danger has become organized around those appraisals. The memory itself had begun to feel like danger arriving in the present, so that when it broke through she no longer experienced it as something finished and over, but as something still happening in her body. Eileen sits with her back against a wall whenever she can, scanning the room so that no one can come up behind her, and she frequently looks over her shoulder as though someone might be following her. After the image broke through, she found herself thinking that if it could still arrive so sharply, there must be something deeply wrong with her, and that thought made her more certain that she was permanently changed. In the workplace, where she still tries to do bookkeeping and audit-related tasks in a small office, she chooses seats that give her a clear view of the door and avoids being trapped in the middle of a meeting room; the smell of sweat from a crowded corridor or the sudden ease of a calm afternoon can be enough to make her tense, alert, and ready to bolt. Keeping herself positioned that way has brought only brief relief, and it has also convinced her that she cannot manage without constant precautions, which only strengthens her belief that the danger is still there. What frightens her most is that if she relaxes, she will be caught off guard again, and that fear has begun to shape her behavior in risky, almost self-defeating ways, as though she were testing whether danger will find her anyway. Even while she is trying to keep herself safe, her mind stays on guard, and every glance behind her or shift of a chair back toward the wall seems to confirm how unsafe she feels. These strategies, however, have not settled her. The rehearsing of conversations before any interaction has made even simple exchanges feel loaded and unnatural, and she often leaves the encounter more aware of herself than of the other person, more convinced that others can tell something happened to her. Her repeated mental reviews of how it could have been prevented and why it happened to her have not brought relief; they have deepened her hopelessness and made her feel that normal emotions are no longer available to her. Each time the memory returns, she becomes more vigilant, and that vigilance, in turn, pulls the images back into focus, so that the photographs in her mind and the bodily feeling of being watched keep reappearing together. The cycle has narrowed her world and made her husband worry, because she is less able to settle into ordinary conversation, more easily startled by the atmosphere of a room, and increasingly withdrawn from the very moments of feeling safe that once gave her some respite. By the time she sought help, Eileen said she was exhausted by the constant effort of bracing herself, replaying the event, and trying to keep her composure in public. She wanted relief from the sense that her face betrays what happened to her and from the conviction that she will never feel normal again, but she was also afraid that if she stopped checking, stopped replaying, or stopped positioning herself defensively, the memory would flood back with the force of the war zone all over again. Once that sense of danger takes hold, the memory seems to come with it; on those high-alert moments, the photographs in her mind surface fully formed, as if her body is still living inside the bombing and the separation from her husband.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly show negative appraisals driving the traumatic memory to become more vivid or recurrent in the same paragraph.
It does not clearly state that the memory leads to maladaptive strategies; instead, strategies are described as responses to danger and appraisals.
The vignette does not explicitly show the traumatic memory itself causing the sense of threat.
It does not clearly state that the traumatic memory produces the negative appraisals, only that appraisals arise from reminders and rumination.
The vignette does not show the sense of threat causing the traumatic memory to return.
It does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies bring back the memory; vigilance is said to pull images back, but the strategies are not directly linked causally enough to the memory.
It does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies generate negative appraisals.
The vignette does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies themselves increase the sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show negative appraisals driving the traumatic memory to become more vivid or recurrent in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: It does not clearly state that the memory leads to maladaptive strategies; instead, strategies are described as responses to danger and appraisals.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette does not explicitly show the traumatic memory itself causing the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: It does not clearly state that the traumatic memory produces the negative appraisals, only that appraisals arise from reminders and rumination.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show the sense of threat causing the traumatic memory to return.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: It does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies bring back the memory; vigilance is said to pull images back, but the strategies are not directly linked causally enough to the memory.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: It does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies generate negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not clearly show that the maladaptive strategies themselves increase the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
